title: Causal Discovery via Quantile Partial Effect
one_liner: Identify which variable causes which by examining how one variable's distribution changes at different values of another, skipping the need to model what causes what internally.
lead: Finding causal direction (does X cause Y or does Y cause X?) usually means building a model of how one variable depends on the other — a hard, error-prone guess. This paper finds cause and effect by looking only at the raw observed data itself: it measures a hidden shape property that tells cause from effect, without ever building an internal model. The measure is called Quantile Partial Effect, or QPE.

problem.h2: Cause vs effect is hard to tell from data alone
paras: When you see two variables that move together — say, ice cream sales and sunburn cases — you know one affects the other. But which way? Does warm weather drive ice cream sales, or does selling more ice cream somehow make it warmer? To answer this, scientists usually guess a model: assume ice cream sales depend on temperature plus some random noise, then check if that model is plausible. The problem is these guesses are fragile. Pick the wrong functional form (maybe the relationship is curved, not linear) or ignore an unmeasured confounder (both variables rise because summer is coming), and your causal direction flips.

A beginner might try fitting both directions and picking the one with better fit. But that fails because both a model of Y depending on X and a model of X depending on Y can achieve equally good fit to the same data — fitting does not reveal which dependency is causal. Adding unmeasured confounders (hidden variables that influence both X and Y) makes the problem even more ambiguous. The core obstacle is that fitting the data tells you how the variables correlate, but not which one is the root cause.

callout.html: Instead of guessing the causal mechanism, measure an asymmetry property (Quantile Partial Effect) directly from the observed data distribution, which points to the true cause.

panels.title: 1. Two variables move together
panels.caption: We see X and Y correlate but don't know: does X cause Y, or Y cause X?

panels.title: 2. Old way: build an inner model
panels.viz_args: Guess: Y = f(X, noise). Check if plausible.
panels.caption: Fit a mechanism. But this guess can be wrong, confusing the causal direction.

panels.title: 3. New way: look at shape asymmetry
panels.caption: Measure how the outcome's distribution changes at different input values.

panels.title: 4. Quantile Partial Effect differs by direction
panels.viz_args: Cause's QPE has a specific shape; effect's QPE does not.
panels.caption: The cause-to-effect path leaves a distinctive fingerprint in the data.

panels.title: 5. Direction found without modeling internals
panels.caption: Identify the true cause by testing which direction matches the shape signature.

steps.text: Collect measurements of X and Y together, no models.
At each value of X, find the quantiles (0.1th, 0.5th, 0.9th percentile) of the Y values.
Compute how the quantile curves change across X values; this is QPE, a shape property of Y given X.

steps.b: Step 4: Test if QPE lies in a finite basis.
steps.text: Check if QPE can be written as a weighted combo of known basis functions; if yes, X causes Y.
The direction where this basis property holds is the true cause; the other is the effect.

paras: Instead of guessing internal mechanisms (how one variable depends on another plus randomness), the paper measures a pure distribution property: Quantile Partial Effect, or the shape of how the outcome's percentiles vary with the input. This QPE lives entirely in the observed data, independent of any assumed model.

hidden.h2: Quantile Partial Effect: the shape fingerprint
hidden.name: Quantile Partial Effect (QPE)
paras: Quantile Partial Effect measures the slope of the conditional quantile curves — that is, how the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of an outcome change as an input variable changes. It is a pure property of the observed data distribution, requiring no guess about internal causality or noise.

The paper uses QPE to test whether cause and effect are identifiable: it assumes that the QPE curves lie within a finite linear span (can be written as a weighted sum of known basis functions). When X causes Y, this constraint on QPE holds; when X is the effect, the constraint fails. By testing which direction satisfies this property, the algorithm identifies the causal direction.

heat.caption: Darker regions show where Quantile Partial Effect is strong; highlight marks regions with distinctive asymmetry.

reads.html: The Quantile Partial Effect is the shape of how the outcome's distribution spreads at each input level. A cause leaves a recognizable fingerprint in this shape.

For each variable X and effect variable Y, the quantile partial effect measures the slope (how fast the percentiles change) of the conditional quantile function. Identifiability holds when this effect lies in a finite linear combination of known basis functions.

mechanism.h2: Why measuring shape discovers cause and effect
paras: When X causes Y, the distribution of Y at each X value has a specific structure: the quantiles (percentiles) of Y curve in a way that can be written as a weighted sum of basis functions. This is not an accident; it follows from the asymmetry of how causes flow into effects through data.

When Y causes X instead, the Quantile Partial Effect of Y on X does not have this finite-span property. The constraint fails. This asymmetry — one direction satisfies the basis constraint, the other does not — arises purely from the shape of the observed distribution, without needing to guess or model any internal mechanism, noise, or causality assumption. The paper proves this mathematically and uses basis function testing to detect which direction has the constraint, thus identifying the true cause.

stages.s: Compute conditional quantiles of Y given X
Test if QPE fits known basis functions
Causal direction: which way satisfies the constraint

math.h2: One readable equation and its meaning
math.words: For each variable X and outcome Y: if the Quantile Partial Effect psi can be written as a weighted sum of basis functions (lies in span of phi), then X causes Y.
math.equation: psi_Y|X(y|x) = sum_j c_j * phi_j(y) implies X -> Y
symbols: Quantile Partial Effect: how Y's percentiles curve with X
weight on the j-th basis function
all possible weighted combinations of the basis functions
X is the cause, Y is the effect

worked.title: Tiny worked example: two basis functions
lines: Suppose we observe X (temperature) and Y (ice cream sales).
The QPE (how these percentiles change per degree) varies smoothly.
Test: can QPE be written as 0.5*polynomial(y) + 0.3*spline(y)? YES for X->Y.
Test the reverse (Y->X, predicting temperature from sales): NO, the basis fit fails.

math.note: The basis-span constraint on QPE is the asymmetry that lets us identify cause from effect in pure data.

bars.h2: How well it finds causal direction

charts.title: Naive method (fit both ways)
charts.note: Fitting both directions often yields the same loss, so you cannot tell which is right.

charts.title: This paper (QPE basis test)
rows: Basis constraint test on causal direction
Basis test fails on wrong direction
charts.note: The basis property is asymmetric: only the true cause satisfies it, making direction unambiguous.

items.b: QPE does not lie in the assumed basis.
items.html: If the true Quantile Partial Effect cannot be written as a weighted sum of your chosen basis functions (polynomials, splines, etc.), the test fails. Choosing a richer basis (more basis functions) helps because it can express more complex shapes, but adds computational cost when fitting more functions to the data.

items.b: Unmeasured confounders that affect both X and Y.
items.html: If a hidden variable U causes both X and Y, the observational distribution is warped. The paper assumes no such latent confounders (causal sufficiency); if they exist, the method may misidentify direction.

items.b: Finite sample noise in quantile estimation.
items.html: Estimating quantiles from data requires many samples per region of X. With sparse data, quantile curves are noisy, and the QPE may not cleanly fit the basis, leading to wrong causal direction.

With enough samples, a well-chosen basis, and no latent confounders, the Quantile Partial Effect test reliably identifies the true causal direction, because the basis constraint is fundamentally asymmetric between cause and effect.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate synthetic data where X causes Y via a nonlinear relationship (e.g., a curved or wavy dependency with added noise). Also generate the reverse where Y causes X. For each pair, estimate the Quantile Partial Effect at a grid of X (or Y) values. Fit basis functions (e.g., polynomial or spline basis) to the QPE curves in both directions. Check: does the basis fit succeed in the true causal direction and fail in the reverse direction?
demo.closing: The demo must show that only the true cause has QPE that fits the basis, reliably distinguishing cause from effect on data where the true causal graph is known.
